questions.q: What does API stand for?
questions.e: An API is a set of rules that lets one program talk to another.

questions.q: What does SQL stand for?
questions.e: SQL is the language used to query and manage relational databases.

questions.q: What does IP stand for in 'IP address'?
questions.e: An IP address identifies a device on a network using the Internet Protocol.

questions.q: What does MPI stand for in parallel computing?
questions.e: MPI is a standard for processes to exchange messages while running in parallel.

questions.q: What does ICMP stand for?
questions.e: ICMP carries error and status messages. The ping command uses it.

questions.q: What does URL stand for?
questions.e: A URL is the address of a resource on the web.

questions.q: What does HTML stand for?
questions.e: HTML describes the structure of a web page.

questions.q: What does CSS stand for?
questions.e: CSS controls how web pages look: colours, fonts and layout.

questions.q: What does HTTP stand for?
questions.e: HTTP is the protocol browsers use to request web pages.

questions.q: What does FTP stand for?
questions.e: FTP moves files between computers over a network.

questions.q: What does DNS stand for?
questions.e: DNS turns names such as example.com into IP addresses.

questions.q: What does DHCP stand for?
questions.e: DHCP gives devices their IP addresses automatically.

questions.q: What does VPN stand for?
questions.e: A VPN makes a secure, private connection over a public network.

questions.q: What does BIOS stand for?
questions.e: BIOS is firmware that starts the computer and loads the operating system.

questions.q: What does GUI stand for?
questions.e: A GUI lets users work with windows, icons and menus instead of typed commands.

questions.q: What does ISP stand for?
questions.e: An ISP is a company that sells internet access.

questions.q: What does IDE stand for in programming?
questions.e: An IDE combines a code editor, compiler and debugger in one tool.

questions.q: What do the letters in ACID stand for in databases?
questions.e: ACID properties keep database transactions reliable.

questions.q: What does CRUD stand for?
questions.e: CRUD names the four basic operations on stored data.

questions.q: What does JSON stand for?
questions.e: JSON is a light text format for exchanging data.

questions.q: What does ASCII stand for?
o: Advanced System Code for Internet Information
American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Automatic Symbol Code for Information Input
questions.e: ASCII maps characters to numbers, such as A = 65.

questions.q: What does SMTP stand for?
questions.e: SMTP is used to send email.

questions.q: What does TCP stand for?
questions.e: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery of data.

questions.q: In cybersecurity, what does APT stand for?
questions.e: An APT is a long, targeted attack that stays hidden in a network.

questions.q: What does DDoS stand for?
questions.e: A DDoS attack floods a service with traffic from many machines.

questions.q: What does SDLC stand for?
questions.e: The SDLC is the set of phases a software project goes through.

questions.q: What does NAT stand for?
questions.e: NAT lets many private devices share one public IP address.

questions.q: What does ARP stand for?
questions.e: ARP finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address.

questions.q: What does SSH stand for?
questions.e: SSH gives an encrypted way to log in to another computer.

questions.q: What does SaaS stand for?
questions.e: With SaaS you use software over the internet, such as Gmail.

questions.q: What does GPU stand for?
questions.e: A GPU handles graphics and many parallel calculations.

questions.q: What does VCS stand for in software development?
questions.e: A VCS records changes to files over time. Git is one.

questions.q: What does IoT stand for?
questions.e: IoT means everyday devices connected to the internet.

questions.q: What does LAN stand for?
questions.e: A LAN connects devices in a small area such as a home or office.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1010?
What is the decimal value of binary 1111?
What is the decimal value of binary 11111111?
questions.e: Eight ones = 2^8 - 1 = 255.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of binary 10000000?
questions.e: Only the eighth bit is set, which is 2^7 = 128.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of binary 101010?
What is the binary form of decimal 13?
What is the binary form of decimal 25?
What is the binary form of decimal 64?
questions.e: 64 = 2^6, so a 1 followed by six zeros.

questions.q: What is the hexadecimal form of decimal 255?
What is the hexadecimal digit for decimal 10?
questions.e: Hex digits run 0-9 then A=10, B=11, up to F=15.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of hexadecimal 1F?
What is the decimal value of hexadecimal 2A?
What is the decimal value of octal 17?
questions.e: 17 in octal = 1 x 8 + 7 = 15.

questions.q: What is the binary form of the hexadecimal digit F?
What is the binary form of the octal digit 7?
What is the result of adding binary 101 and 11?
questions.e: 5 + 3 = 8, which is 1000 in binary.

questions.q: How many bits are in one byte?
questions.e: A byte is 8 bits.

questions.q: How many bits are in a nibble?
questions.e: A nibble is half a byte, so 4 bits.

questions.q: How many bytes are in one kilobyte (KB) in computing?
questions.e: In binary computing 1 KB = 2^10 = 1024 bytes.

questions.q: How many kilobytes are in one megabyte (MB) in computing?
What is the largest unsigned number that 8 bits can store?
questions.e: n bits store up to 2^n - 1, so 255.

questions.q: How many different values can 3 bits represent?
questions.e: 2^3 = 8 values (0 to 7).

questions.q: What is the largest unsigned number that 4 bits can store?
What is the ASCII code of the capital letter 'A'?
questions.e: Capital letters start at 65. Small 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48.

questions.q: What is the ASCII code of the small letter 'a'?
questions.e: Small letters start at 97.

questions.q: What is the 4-bit two's complement form of -5?
questions.e: 5 is 0101. Invert to 1010 and add 1 to get 1011.

questions.q: Which number system uses only the digits 0 and 1?
questions.e: Binary is base 2.

questions.q: What is the base of the octal number system?
questions.e: Octal uses the digits 0 to 7.

questions.q: What is the base of the hexadecimal number system?
questions.e: Hexadecimal uses 0-9 and A-F.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of binary 110?
What is the smallest unit of data in a computer?
questions.e: A bit is a single 0 or 1.

questions.q: Which of these units is the largest?
questions.e: KB < MB < GB < TB.

questions.q: What is decimal 16 written in hexadecimal?
questions.e: 16 = 1 x 16 + 0, so 10 in hex.

questions.q: How many layers does the OSI model have?
questions.e: The OSI model has seven layers.

questions.q: Which is the top layer of the OSI model?
questions.e: Layer 7 is Application, closest to the user.

questions.q: Which is the bottom layer of the OSI model?
questions.e: Layer 1 is the Physical layer: cables, signals and bits.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for IP addressing and routing?
questions.e: Layer 3, the Network layer, moves packets between networks.

questions.q: Which OSI layer provides end-to-end delivery, as TCP and UDP do?
questions.e: Layer 4 is the Transport layer.

questions.q: Which OSI layer uses MAC addresses?
questions.e: Layer 2 handles frames and MAC addresses on a local network.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles data encryption, compression and formatting?
questions.e: Layer 6, the Presentation layer, translates and secures data.

questions.q: Which OSI layer sets up, manages and ends sessions between applications?
questions.e: Layer 5 is the Session layer.

questions.q: Which list shows the OSI layers from layer 7 down to layer 1?
o: Application, Session, Presentation, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Application, Presentation, Transport, Session, Network, Data Link, Physical
questions.e: A handy memory phrase: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

questions.q: At which OSI layer does a router work?
questions.e: Routers forward packets using IP addresses, which is layer 3.

questions.q: At which OSI layer does a switch normally work?
questions.e: A switch forwards frames using MAC addresses, which is layer 2.

questions.q: At which OSI layer does a hub work?
questions.e: A hub just repeats electrical signals, which is layer 1.

questions.q: What is the data unit called at the Data Link layer?
questions.e: Physical: bits, Data Link: frames, Network: packets, Transport: segments.

questions.q: What is the data unit called at the Network layer?
questions.e: Network layer data is called a packet.

questions.q: What is the data unit called at the Transport layer for TCP?
questions.e: TCP data at the Transport layer is a segment.

questions.q: Which protocol gives reliable, connection-oriented delivery?
questions.e: TCP sets up a connection and resends lost data.

questions.q: Which protocol is connectionless and often used for live video and gaming?
questions.e: UDP is fast because it skips connection setup and re-sending.

questions.q: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
questions.e: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK.

questions.q: Which protocol finds the MAC address that matches an IP address?
questions.e: ARP maps an IP address to a MAC address on a local network.

questions.q: Which protocol converts a domain name into an IP address?
questions.e: DNS is the internet's phone book.

questions.q: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses to devices?
questions.e: DHCP hands out IP addresses so you do not set them by hand.

questions.q: Which protocol does the ping command use?
questions.e: Ping sends ICMP echo requests to test reachability.

questions.q: What does the ping command do?
o: Lists all devices on a network
Checks whether a host is reachable and measures the round-trip time
questions.e: Ping sends a small message and times the reply.

questions.q: Which port does HTTP use by default?
questions.e: HTTP uses port 80.

questions.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.e: HTTPS uses port 443.

questions.q: Which port does FTP use for control by default?
questions.e: FTP control uses port 21.

questions.q: Which port does SSH use by default?
questions.e: SSH uses port 22.

questions.q: Which port does SMTP use by default?
questions.e: SMTP uses port 25.

questions.q: Which port does DNS use by default?
questions.e: DNS uses port 53.

questions.q: Which port does Telnet use by default?
questions.e: Telnet uses port 23, and it is not encrypted.

questions.q: Which protocol is used for secure file transfer carried over SSH?
questions.e: SFTP is FTP-like transfer carried inside SSH.

questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
questions.e: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, such as 192.168.1.1.

questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
questions.e: IPv6 uses 128 bits to give a huge number of addresses.

questions.q: How many bits are in a MAC address?
questions.e: A MAC address is 48 bits, shown as six hex pairs.

questions.q: What is the loopback IP address of a computer?
questions.e: 127.0.0.1 always points back to the same machine.

questions.q: Which of these is a private IP address?
Which IP address class covers 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255?
questions.e: Class A starts 1-126, Class B 128-191, Class C 192-223.

questions.q: What is the subnet mask for a /24 network?
What is the subnet mask for a /16 network?
questions.e: 16 bits of ones = 255.255.0.0.

questions.q: What is the subnet mask for a /20 network?
questions.e: 20 bits of ones: the third octet is 11110000 = 240.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /24 network have?
questions.e: 256 addresses minus the network and broadcast addresses.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /26 network have?
questions.e: 2^6 = 64 addresses minus 2 = 62.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /30 network have?
questions.e: 2^2 = 4 addresses minus 2 = 2.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /29 network have?
questions.e: 2^3 = 8 addresses minus 2 = 6.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /22 network have?
questions.e: 2^10 = 1024 addresses minus 2 = 1022.

questions.q: How many subnets do you get by splitting a /24 network into /26 networks?
questions.e: /26 borrows 2 bits from /24, and 2^2 = 4.

questions.q: What is the broadcast address of the subnet 192.168.5.64/26?
questions.e: A /26 block holds 64 addresses: .64 to .127, and .127 is the broadcast.

questions.q: What is the first usable address in the subnet 10.0.0.0/30?
questions.e: 10.0.0.0 is the network address, so the first usable one is 10.0.0.1.

questions.q: What is the last usable address in the subnet 172.16.50.0/23?
questions.e: The block runs 172.16.50.0 to 172.16.51.255. The last usable is one below the broadcast.

questions.q: Which topology connects every device to a central switch or hub?
questions.e: In a star topology each device has its own link to the centre.

questions.q: Which topology uses a single shared cable for all devices?
questions.e: All devices tap into one backbone cable.

questions.q: Which topology gives the most fault tolerance because every device links to every other?
questions.e: Full mesh has many paths, so one failure does not stop traffic.

questions.q: Which device connects different networks and forwards packets between them?
questions.e: A router joins networks and chooses the path for packets.

questions.q: Which device connects devices inside one LAN and uses MAC addresses to forward frames?
questions.e: A switch sends frames only to the port of the destination device.

questions.q: Which device converts digital signals to analogue signals and back for the internet line?
questions.e: Modem stands for modulator-demodulator.

questions.q: Which routing protocol uses hop count as its metric?
questions.e: RIP counts hops and allows at most 15.

questions.q: Which network type covers a whole city?
questions.e: A Metropolitan Area Network covers a city or large campus.

questions.q: Which wireless standard family does Wi-Fi follow?
questions.e: 802.11 is Wi-Fi, and 802.3 is Ethernet.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a subnet mask?
o: To split an IP address into network and host parts
questions.e: The mask shows which bits identify the network and which identify the host.

questions.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic
questions.e: A firewall allows or blocks traffic using security rules.

questions.q: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have?
questions.e: Application, Transport, Internet and Network Access.

questions.q: What is bandwidth?
o: The physical length of a cable
The amount of data a connection can carry per second
The number of devices on a network
questions.e: Bandwidth is measured in bits per second.

questions.q: What do the letters CIA stand for in the security triad?
questions.e: Keep data private, keep it correct, and keep it available when needed.

questions.q: Which security principle means information is not shown to unauthorised people?
questions.e: Confidentiality keeps secrets secret.

questions.q: Which security principle means data is not changed without permission?
questions.e: Integrity means the data stays accurate and unaltered.

questions.q: Which security principle means systems and data can be used when needed?
questions.e: A DDoS attack targets availability.

questions.q: Which malware copies itself and spreads across a network without a host file?
questions.e: Worms spread on their own, while viruses attach to files.

questions.q: Which malware attaches itself to a program or file and spreads when that file is run?
questions.e: A virus needs a host file to spread.

questions.q: Which malware pretends to be useful software but does harm?
questions.e: Named after the Trojan horse, it tricks the user into installing it.

questions.q: Which malware locks or encrypts your files and demands payment?
questions.e: Ransomware holds data hostage until a ransom is paid.

questions.q: Which malware secretly collects information about what a user does?
questions.e: Spyware watches activity and sends it to an attacker.

questions.q: Which malware shows unwanted adverts?
questions.e: Adware floods the user with pop-ups and banners.

questions.q: Which malware runs its harmful code only when a set condition is met, such as a date?
questions.e: A logic bomb waits for a trigger before it acts.

questions.q: Which malware hides itself deep in the system and gives an attacker hidden control?
questions.e: Rootkits conceal other malware and their own presence.

questions.q: What does a keylogger do?
o: Records the keys a user types
questions.e: Keyloggers capture passwords and messages as they are typed.

questions.q: What is a botnet?
o: A network of infected computers controlled by an attacker
questions.e: Botnets are often used to launch DDoS attacks.

questions.q: What is phishing?
o: Encrypting data with a public key
Tricking people into giving personal information using fake emails or websites
Copying files to a backup drive
questions.e: Phishing relies on deception, not technical force.

questions.q: What is a DDoS attack?
o: Flooding a service with traffic from many sources so it becomes unavailable
questions.e: The aim is to make the service unusable for real users.

questions.q: What is SQL injection?
o: Sending too many emails to a server
Guessing passwords by trying many words
Copying a website to steal its design
Inserting malicious SQL code through an input field to attack a database
questions.e: It works when an application builds queries from unchecked user input.

questions.q: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
o: Two servers sharing the same IP address
A virus that hides in email attachments
An attacker secretly intercepts communication between two parties
questions.e: The attacker can read or change messages without either side knowing.

questions.q: What is a brute-force attack?
o: Trying many passwords or keys until one works
questions.e: Long, random passwords make brute force much slower.

questions.q: What is social engineering?
o: Manipulating people into giving up confidential information
questions.e: It attacks people rather than machines.

questions.q: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
o: A flaw fixed on the day it is found
A flaw that attackers exploit before the vendor knows or has a fix
A virus that deletes itself in a day
questions.e: The vendor has had zero days to fix it.

questions.q: Which of these is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
questions.e: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to lock and unlock. AES and DES are examples.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a symmetric encryption algorithm?
questions.e: RSA is asymmetric: it uses a public and a private key.

questions.q: In public key encryption, which key does a sender use to encrypt a message for you?
questions.e: Only your private key can decrypt what your public key locked.

questions.q: Which key must be kept secret in public key cryptography?
questions.e: The public key can be shared freely.

questions.q: Which of these is a hashing algorithm?
questions.e: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length output that cannot be reversed.

questions.q: What is a key property of a secure hash function?
o: It can be reversed with the right key
Its output length grows with the input
It is easy to find two inputs with the same output
It gives a fixed-length output and cannot be reversed
questions.e: Hashes are one-way and resistant to collisions.

questions.q: What does salting do in password storage?
o: Adds random data to a password before hashing it
Turns the password into plain text
questions.e: Salts make identical passwords produce different hashes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a digital signature?
o: To hide the message from everyone
To prove who sent a message and that it was not changed
questions.e: It gives authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.

questions.q: Which protocol encrypts web traffic?
questions.e: HTTPS is HTTP carried over SSL/TLS.

questions.q: What is two-factor authentication?
o: Using two different kinds of proof to log in
Using two passwords of the same kind
Logging in from two devices at once
questions.e: For example a password plus a code sent to your phone.

questions.q: Which password habit is strong?
o: A long mix of letters, numbers and symbols that is not reused
The same password for all accounts
questions.e: Length and uniqueness make passwords hard to guess.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
o: Authentication decides what you may do, authorisation proves who you are
Authentication is encryption, authorisation is hashing
Authentication proves who you are, authorisation decides what you may do
questions.e: First you log in, then the system checks your permissions.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a penetration test?
o: To find weaknesses in a system by safely attacking it
questions.e: Ethical hackers test defences before real attackers do.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
o: Let users choose their own access
Give users only the access they need for their job
questions.e: It limits the damage if an account is misused.

questions.q: What is steganography?
o: Hiding a secret message inside another file such as an image
questions.e: The message is hidden so nobody knows it exists.

questions.q: What is a honeypot?
o: A decoy system set up to attract and study attackers
questions.e: It lets defenders watch attacker behaviour safely.

questions.q: What does a VPN mainly provide?
o: An encrypted, private connection over a public network
questions.e: It hides traffic from others on the same network.

questions.q: What is IP spoofing?
o: Faking the source IP address of packets
questions.e: Attackers use it to hide their identity or pretend to be another device.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a version control system?
o: To track changes to files over time and let people work together
questions.e: You can go back to earlier versions and merge teammates' work.

questions.q: What is Git?
questions.e: Every developer has a full copy of the project history.

questions.q: What is GitHub?
o: A website that hosts Git repositories online
questions.e: Git is the tool, and GitHub is a service built around it.

questions.q: Which command creates a new Git repository?
questions.e: git init sets up Git tracking in the current folder.

questions.q: Which command copies an existing remote repository to your computer?
questions.e: git clone downloads the repository with its full history.

questions.q: Which command moves changes into the staging area?
questions.e: Staging chooses which changes go into the next commit.

questions.q: Which command saves staged changes as a new snapshot in the history?
questions.e: A commit records the staged changes with a message.

questions.q: Which command sends your local commits to a remote repository?
questions.e: git push uploads your commits to the remote.

questions.q: Which command downloads and merges changes from a remote repository?
questions.e: git pull is a fetch followed by a merge.

questions.q: Which command downloads remote changes without merging them?
questions.e: git fetch only updates your view of the remote.

questions.q: Which command shows which files are changed, staged or untracked?
questions.e: git status summarises the current state of the working folder.

questions.q: Which command shows the history of commits?
questions.e: git log lists commits with author, date and message.

questions.q: Which command shows the exact line changes that have not been staged?
questions.e: git diff compares the working files with the last staged or committed version.

questions.q: Which command creates or lists branches?
questions.e: A branch is a separate line of development.

questions.q: Which command combines the history of another branch into the current branch?
questions.e: git merge brings two lines of work together.

questions.q: What is a merge conflict?
o: When two repositories have the same name
When a commit message is empty
When Git cannot combine changes because both branches changed the same lines
questions.e: You must edit the file by hand and choose what to keep.

questions.q: What does the .gitignore file do?
o: Lists files and folders that Git should not track
questions.e: Useful for build output, secrets and temporary files.

questions.q: What is the staging area in Git?
o: A place where you prepare changes before committing them
questions.e: It lets you commit only some of your changes.

questions.q: What does git stash do?
o: Temporarily saves uncommitted changes so you can switch work
questions.e: You can bring the changes back later with git stash pop.

questions.q: What is a pull request?
o: A request to delete a repository
A request to review and merge your branch into another branch
A message to the server administrator
questions.e: It is how teams review code before merging.

questions.q: What is a fork on GitHub?
o: Your own copy of another person's repository
questions.e: Forks let you change a project without touching the original.

questions.q: What is 'origin' in Git?
o: The default name of the remote repository
questions.e: git clone sets the source as origin.

questions.q: Which of these is a centralised version control system?
questions.e: In a centralised system there is one main server holding the history.

questions.q: What does HEAD mean in Git?
o: A pointer to the current commit or branch you are on
questions.e: HEAD tells Git where you are working now.

questions.q: Which command safely undoes a commit by creating a new commit that reverses it?
questions.e: git revert keeps the history, so it is safe on shared branches.

questions.q: What does a compiler do?
o: Runs source code one line at a time
Translates the whole source code into machine code before it runs
questions.e: C and C++ programs are usually compiled.

questions.q: What does an interpreter do?
o: Translates the whole program at once into a file
Runs source code line by line without producing a separate machine code file first
questions.e: Python and JavaScript are usually interpreted.

questions.q: What does an assembler do?
o: Converts assembly language into machine code
questions.e: Assembly is a low-level language with short codes for CPU instructions.

questions.q: In what form does a CPU directly understand instructions?
questions.e: Everything must finally become binary machine code.

questions.q: Which of these is a high-level language?
questions.e: High-level languages are closer to human language.

questions.q: Which language is used to build the structure of a web page?
questions.e: HTML is the markup that defines headings, paragraphs and links.

questions.q: Which language is used to style a web page?
questions.e: CSS controls colours, fonts and layout.

questions.q: Which language mainly makes web pages interactive in the browser?
questions.e: JavaScript runs in the browser and responds to user actions.

questions.q: Which of these is a scripting language?
questions.e: Scripting languages are usually interpreted at run time. Python and PHP are also examples.

questions.q: Which language is widely used for data analysis and machine learning?
questions.e: Python has many libraries for data and AI.

questions.q: Which language is officially recommended by Google for new Android apps?
questions.e: Java is also widely used on Android. Swift is for Apple devices.

questions.q: Which language is used mainly to build iPhone apps?
questions.e: Swift replaced Objective-C as Apple's main language.

questions.q: Which language is used to query a relational database?
questions.e: SQL stores, finds and changes data in tables.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an API?
o: To let one piece of software talk to another using agreed rules
questions.e: For example a weather app asks a weather service for data through its API.

questions.q: What is a variable in programming?
o: A fixed value that never changes
A named place in memory that stores a value
questions.e: The value of a variable can change while the program runs.

questions.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem
questions.e: Algorithms are written as flowcharts or pseudocode before coding.

questions.q: What is debugging?
o: Finding and fixing errors in a program
questions.e: A bug is a mistake that makes a program behave wrongly.

questions.q: Which error is a mistake in the rules of the language, such as a missing bracket?
questions.e: The compiler or interpreter reports syntax errors before the program runs.

questions.q: Which error lets a program run but gives wrong results?
questions.e: The code is valid, but the idea behind it is wrong.

questions.q: Which error happens while the program is running, such as dividing by zero?
questions.e: It stops the program during execution.

questions.q: What is polymorphism in object-oriented programming?
o: Building a class from another class
The same operation behaving differently for different objects
Writing the program in many languages
questions.e: Overloading and overriding are ways to achieve it.

questions.q: What is encapsulation in object-oriented programming?
o: Bundling data and methods together and hiding the details
questions.e: Private fields with public methods are an example.

questions.q: What is inheritance in object-oriented programming?
o: A class receiving the properties and methods of another class
questions.e: A child class reuses code from its parent class.

questions.q: What is recursion?
questions.e: Every recursive function needs a base case to stop.

questions.q: Which data structure is used to handle function calls in recursion?
questions.e: The call stack remembers where each call must return.

questions.q: Which data structure follows first in, first out (FIFO)?
questions.e: The first item added is the first removed, like a line of people.

questions.q: Which data structure follows last in, first out (LIFO)?
questions.e: The last item added is the first removed, like a stack of plates.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
questions.e: Each step halves the search area.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code means the request was successful?
questions.e: 200 OK means everything worked.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code means 'Not Found'?
questions.e: The server cannot find the requested page.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code means an internal server error?
questions.e: 500 means something went wrong on the server.

questions.q: Which HTTP status code means access is forbidden?
questions.e: The server understood the request but refuses it.

questions.q: What does 'responsive design' mean in web development?
o: Pages that adapt to different screen sizes
questions.e: The same page works on phone, tablet and desktop.

questions.q: What is JSON mainly used for?
o: Exchanging data between systems in a light text format
questions.e: APIs commonly send and receive JSON.

questions.q: What is the SDLC phase order that is correct?
questions.e: You must know what to build before you design, code and test it.

questions.q: Which Agile value is correct?
o: Following a plan over responding to change
Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
questions.e: The Agile Manifesto values working software more.

questions.q: What is the Waterfall model?
o: A model with short repeated cycles
A sequence where each phase finishes before the next begins
questions.e: Waterfall flows in one direction, like water down steps.

questions.q: What is the purpose of boundary value analysis in testing?
o: To test values at the edges of input ranges
To test how fast a system runs
questions.e: Bugs often appear at the minimum and maximum values.

questions.q: What does npm stand for and manage?
o: Node Package Manager, which manages JavaScript packages
New Project Maker, which creates projects
Network Protocol Monitor, which watches traffic
Node Process Manager, which runs servers
questions.e: npm installs libraries that JavaScript projects use.

questions.q: What is the CPU often called?
questions.e: The CPU carries out program instructions.

questions.q: What does the ALU do?
questions.e: ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit.

questions.q: What does the control unit do?
o: Directs the flow of instructions and data inside the CPU
questions.e: It fetches, decodes and coordinates execution.

questions.q: Which memory is volatile, meaning it loses its data when power is off?
questions.e: RAM holds working data and is cleared when the computer shuts down.

questions.q: Which memory keeps its contents when power is off and holds start-up instructions?
questions.e: ROM stores firmware such as the BIOS.

questions.q: Which is the fastest type of memory in a computer?
questions.e: Registers sit inside the CPU. Cache is next, then RAM.

questions.q: What is cache memory?
o: Very fast memory that keeps frequently used data close to the CPU
Memory that is used only for graphics
questions.e: It reduces the time the CPU waits for data.

questions.q: Which storage has no moving parts?
questions.e: A solid state drive stores data in flash memory chips.

questions.q: What does the motherboard do?
o: Connects and lets all computer parts communicate
questions.e: CPU, RAM and other components all plug into it.

questions.q: Which of these is an input device?
questions.e: Input devices send data to the computer.

questions.q: Which of these is an output device?
questions.e: Output devices show or play results.

questions.q: What is the main job of an operating system?
o: Managing hardware and running programs for the user
questions.e: The OS manages memory, processes, files and devices.

questions.q: Which of these is an operating system?
questions.e: Linux, Windows, macOS and Android are operating systems.

questions.q: What is the kernel?
o: The core part of an operating system that manages hardware and processes
questions.e: Every other part of the OS relies on the kernel.

questions.q: What is a process?
questions.e: A process has its own memory and state.

questions.q: What is a thread?
o: The smallest unit of execution inside a process
questions.e: Threads in the same process share memory.

questions.q: What does a semaphore do in an operating system?
o: Helps processes synchronise and share resources safely
questions.e: It is used to avoid problems when processes use the same resource.

questions.q: What is a deadlock?
o: A process that runs very fast
A situation where processes wait for each other forever
questions.e: Each process holds something another one needs.

questions.q: Which algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance?
questions.e: It grants resources only if the system stays in a safe state.

questions.q: What is virtual memory?
o: A very fast type of cache
Using disk space as an extension of RAM
questions.e: It lets programs use more memory than the RAM installed.

questions.q: What is paging?
o: Dividing memory into fixed-size blocks that can be moved between RAM and disk
Printing a document page by page
questions.e: It lets a program's memory be scattered in physical memory.

questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process a fixed time slice in turn?
questions.e: Round Robin is fair and good for time-sharing systems.

questions.q: Which file system is the default on modern Windows?
questions.e: EXT4 is common on Linux and APFS on Apple devices.

questions.q: Which Linux command lists files and folders?
questions.e: ls lists the contents of a directory.

questions.q: Which Linux command changes the current directory?
questions.e: cd means change directory.

questions.q: Which Linux command shows the current directory?
questions.e: pwd means print working directory.

questions.q: Which Linux command creates a new directory?
questions.e: mkdir means make directory.

questions.q: Which Linux command deletes files?
questions.e: rm means remove.

questions.q: Which Linux command copies files?
questions.e: cp means copy. mv moves or renames.

questions.q: Which Linux command searches for text inside files?
questions.e: grep prints lines that match a pattern.

questions.q: Which Linux command changes file permissions?
questions.e: chmod sets who can read, write or run a file.

questions.q: Which Linux command runs another command with administrator rights?
questions.e: sudo means superuser do.

questions.q: Which command is used to install software packages on Debian and Ubuntu?
questions.e: apt-get installs and updates packages.

questions.q: Which Linux command shows the running processes?
questions.e: ps lists processes. top shows them live.

questions.q: Which key combination copies the selected item in most programs?
questions.e: Ctrl + V pastes, Ctrl + X cuts and Ctrl + Z undoes.

questions.q: What is Artificial Intelligence?
o: Machines doing tasks that normally need human intelligence
questions.e: Examples are learning, reasoning and understanding language.

questions.q: Who is known as the father of artificial intelligence and coined the term in 1956?
questions.e: He organised the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

questions.q: Who proposed the Turing Test?
questions.e: A machine passes if a person cannot tell it from a human in conversation.

questions.q: What is machine learning?
o: Computers learning patterns from data without being told every rule
questions.e: It is a part of AI.

questions.q: In which type of learning does the model train on labelled examples?
questions.e: Each training example comes with the correct answer.

questions.q: Which type of learning finds patterns in data that has no labels?
questions.e: Clustering is a common example.

questions.q: What are neural networks inspired by?
o: The structure of the human brain
The layout of a hard disk
questions.e: They are made of layers of connected nodes.

questions.q: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
o: Teaching computers to understand and use human language
questions.e: Translators and chatbots use NLP.

questions.q: What is computer vision?
o: Teaching computers to understand images and video
questions.e: Face recognition is an example.

questions.q: Which computer beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997?
questions.e: IBM's Deep Blue won a six-game match.

questions.q: Which AI system beat a top human Go player in 2016?
questions.e: AlphaGo, from DeepMind, beat Lee Sedol.

questions.q: What is generative AI?
o: AI that creates new content such as text or images
questions.e: ChatGPT and image generators are examples.

questions.q: What does deep learning use?
questions.e: Many layers allow the model to learn complex patterns.

questions.q: What are the three main Vs of big data?
questions.e: Huge amounts of data, arriving fast, in many forms.

questions.q: What is cloud computing?
o: Storing data only on a USB drive
Using the internet without a computer
Using computing services over the internet instead of owning the hardware
questions.e: You rent storage, servers or software when you need them.

questions.q: Which cloud model gives virtual machines and storage to rent?
questions.e: Infrastructure as a Service gives you computing resources.

questions.q: Which cloud model gives a platform for developers to build and run apps?
questions.e: Platform as a Service hides the servers and operating system.

questions.q: What is cloud elasticity?
o: The ability to scale resources up and down on demand
questions.e: You pay for what you use.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a CDN?
o: Faster delivery of content by serving it from a location near the user
questions.e: CDN stands for Content Delivery Network.

questions.q: What does a container such as Docker provide?
o: A light, portable package that holds an app and what it needs to run
questions.e: Containers run the same way on any machine.

questions.q: What is virtualisation?
o: Running several virtual computers on one physical machine
questions.e: A hypervisor manages the virtual machines.

questions.q: What is the Internet of Things?
o: Everyday devices connected to the internet and sharing data
questions.e: Smart watches and sensors are examples.

questions.q: What technology is behind Bitcoin?
questions.e: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-resistant list of records.

questions.q: Who is known as the father of the computer?
questions.e: He designed the Analytical Engine in the 1800s.

questions.q: Who is considered the first computer programmer?
questions.e: She wrote the first algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

questions.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.e: He created the web in 1989 at CERN.

questions.q: Which was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer?
questions.e: ENIAC was completed in 1945.

questions.q: Which technology marked the first generation of computers?
questions.e: Second generation: transistors. Third: ICs. Fourth: microprocessors.

questions.q: Which technology marked the second generation of computers?
questions.e: Transistors made computers smaller and more reliable.

questions.q: Which technology marked the third generation of computers?
questions.e: Many transistors were placed on a single chip.

questions.q: Which technology marked the fourth generation of computers?
questions.e: A whole CPU on one chip made personal computers possible.

questions.q: What does Moore's law say?
o: The number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years
Computers become half the price every year
questions.e: It has guided chip progress for decades.
